messages.author: e7a767e08a4b2d14
messages.subject: large parameter estimates using 'occu'
parts:
Hi all -

I'm performing a simple single season occupancy model, with response variable as presence/absence.  All state (site) covariates (10) are continuous, while my observation covariates are both continuous and categorical.  While my global model produces parameter estimates in the range of +-5, most nested models generate parameter estimates in the 10's to 100's, even with the detection probs modeled with intercept only, which prevents interpretation of the odds ratios and effect sizes.

Using the standard glm function (excluding and including observation covariates) in R results in parameter estimates typically seen in logistic regression with values ranging around +/- 1.

I know models that use categorical variables only can suffer from this situation if one of the categories is not represented in either of the response outcomes, but this is not the case with my continuous variables.

Has anyone experienced a similar situation, and if so do you have suggestions for a remedy?

Thanks
Patrick

messages.author: 681fb59733e01a1e
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] large parameter estimates using 'occu'
parts:
hi Patrick,
 First, I suggest using the GLM estimates  as starting values  in the occu function.
 If that doesn't resolve the problem then its possible you have a problem with the way your data are organized.  The other possibility is if your data are highly over-dispersed then you can have extreme instability in some parameters -- but usually not in covariate effects, which is why I think its probably some problem with the organization of the data.
regards
andy

messages.author: e7a767e08a4b2d14
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] large parameter estimates using 'occu'
parts:
Hi Andy -

I estimated the dispersion parameter to be 1.3 and used that along with the MuMIn package to compute QAICc and as you suspect it doesn't really impact the value of the parameter estimates much at all.

Using GLM estimates as starting values did not change the final converged values of the parameters either.

Can you be more specific in what you mean by 'organization of the data'?  I've reduced collinearity to acceptable levels by identifying problematic covariates using condition numbers and variance decomposition proportions (Belsley, Kuh, and Welsch (1980)) as implemented in the 'perturb' package in R.  I have also mean centered and scaled all variables.  What other 'data organization' considerations exist?

Thanks for you help
Patrick

Hi Richard -

You may have me confused with another Patrick as I am not traveling to Patuxent.

My sample size is 73 and the number of parameters I'm trying to estimate is 4 prediction and 6 occupancy.  Oddly, the 10 total parameters that are estimated as the global model are more reasonable (+/- 5) compared to reduced models where there may be 5-6 parameters and their estimates go into the 10's and 100's.

I think you're right about one or several parameters near the boundary because only the profile confidence intervals produce intervals that do not bound zero.

Patrick

parts:
Hi Patrick,

Sorry for confusing you with someone else. If a parameter is near a boundary then I don't think there is much to worry about. The inverse logit of 20 is about the same as the inv-logit of 100.

plogis(20)
plogis(100)

So perhaps psi is estimated to be near 1 for some level of a factor, unless you include another covariate effect.... as in your global model.

Of  course there could be some other issue here that I am not aware of.

Richard
